title: Do Students Still Need to Learn Calculus?
author: Liz Cohen
summary: Liz Cohen pushes back against Ted Dintersmith's call to abandon calculus in favor of statistics, arguing that calculus remains foundational to modern technology, scientific discovery, and human ingenuity. She contends that replacing calculus with data science will not improve student outcomes, and that schools should instead build strong foundational math skills from early grades. The goal should be both statistics and calculus, not an either-or trade.
points: Ted Dintersmith's book Aftermath argues calculus is obsolete and schools should pivot entirely to statistics and relevance
Cohen counters that calculus underlies lasers, GPS, LLMs, drug therapy, and virtually every modern invention
Statistics is valuable but swapping it for calculus won't increase the number of students succeeding in advanced math
Early math fluency is essential for later success; Dintersmith ignores this foundational evidence entirely
The pandemic exposed a crumbling math foundation; denying learning loss makes serious reform harder, not easier
quotes: Calculus is the gateway to almost everything we have invented in the last century, to the technology that powers the world, and to the large language models to which many people appear willing to surrender their cognition and humanity.

Math, like reading, is a muscle that must be intentionally developed. You first build the cognitive routines so that when the child gets to more advanced topics, he spends minimal time thinking about the addition, multiplication, or factorization they require.
Part of the value proposition of public education must be to provide access to the hard stuff. Calculus is demanding, and that's a good thing.
If schools instead send a message to students and parents that calculus is unimportant, they will effectively relegate most kids who heed it to working for the ones who took calculus anyway.

These twin challenges of learning loss layered on an already eroding system comprise the true educational emergency for this generation, for the next, and for all who will one day enroll their child in American public schools.
